# The Work and Torah-Ideological Teaching of Rabbi Kalphon Moshe HaCohen of Djerba (1874–1950)

Rabbi Kalphon Moshe HaCohen (1874–1950) was among the most prominent rabbinic scholars and halakhic authorities in the Djerbian Jewish community during the late nineteenth and first half of the twentieth centuries. He served as head of the yeshiva and rabbinical court judge in Hara Kebira, the main Jewish quarter of Djerba, and was renowned for his extensive knowledge of Torah, his penetrating analytical ability, and his prolific literary output. His halakhic rulings and responsa addressed a wide range of questions concerning Jewish law and were recognized as authoritative not only in Djerba but throughout the Jewish communities of North Africa.

Rabbi Kalphon Moshe was born in 1874 into a distinguished rabbinical family in Djerba. He studied under the leading Torah scholars of his generation in Djerba and distinguished himself at a young age through his diligence and exceptional intellectual capabilities. After completing his studies, he was appointed to serve on the rabbinical court and later became head of the yeshiva in Hara Kebira, positions he held until his death in 1950.

His primary halakhic work is the collection of responsa *Vayomer Moshe*, which contains his answers to hundreds of halakhic questions on all four sections of the *Shulhan Arukh*. The work demonstrates profound familiarity with the entire breadth of rabbinic literature—Talmud, Rishonim, and Aharonim—as well as remarkable analytical acuity in clarifying complex halakhic issues. Beyond his halakhic writing, Rabbi Kalphon Moshe also composed works in Jewish thought and ethics that reflect his spiritual worldview and educational philosophy.

The Work and Halakhic and Ideological Teachings of Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen of Djerba (1874–1950)

This report presents an in-depth analysis of the rabbinic and public enterprise of Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen (Moharmakh), who served as chief rabbi and head of the rabbinical court of the Djerba community in southern Tunisia during the first half of the twentieth century. Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen is considered one of the greatest Jewish sages of his generation, and he was known for his efforts to preserve the conservative Torah tradition of Djerba against the influences of modernization and secularization. His massive literary enterprise, which includes approximately one hundred compositions, headed by the responsa series Sho'el ve-Nish'al (One Who Asks and Is Asked) and the book of customs Brit Kehunah (Covenant of the Priesthood), provided a stable framework of halakhic decision-making for Tunisian Jewry. Moreover, his ideological teachings presented a unique combination of rootedness in Zionism and principled opposition to external education, as he advocated making local Torah purity the basis for repairing the world.

The Work and Halakhic and Ideological Teachings of Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen of Djerba (1874–1950)

Introduction and Clarification of the Figure's Identity

This report is dedicated to an in-depth analysis of the enormous enterprise and the halakhic and ideological teachings of the Gaon Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen (known by the acronym Moharmakh), who served as chief rabbi and head of the rabbinical court of the Jewish community on the island of Djerba in southern Tunisia. Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen, who was born on the twelfth of Shevat 5634 (1874) and died on the eighteenth of Tevet 5710 (1950), is considered one of the greatest Jewish sages of the twentieth century and had a decisive influence on the patterns of halakhic decision-making and study among emigrants from all of Tunisia.[1, 2, 3]

It should be noted that although the user's inquiry referred to "Rabbi Haim Kalfon," the research data clearly point to Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen as the central Torah figure from Djerba of his time, whose Torah and public work is the main subject of discussion in both rabbinic literature and academic research.[4, 5] It is possible that the name "Haim" in the query resulted from confusion with figures in his family, such as his father, Rabbi Shalom HaKohen, who composed the book Haim ve-Shalom (Life and Peace) [6], or Eliyahu son of Rabbi Haim Kalfon, who is mentioned as the author of a Hebrew Kabbalistic dictionary.[7] The analysis below will therefore focus on the multifaceted legacy of Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen.

Chapter 1: Introduction and Historical Context – Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen and the World of Djerba

1.1 Djerba – An Island of Tradition in the Modern Era

Understanding the magnitude of Moharmakh's work requires reference to the unique status of the Djerba community. The island of Djerba, situated in southern Tunisia, served in recent centuries as a strong Torah fortress. The Jewish community there succeeded in preserving its traditional and conservative way of life to a considerable degree, standing firmly against the profound transformations that characterized the community centers in northern Tunisia, primarily the capital Tunis, which absorbed modern European influences due to the French protectorate.[4]

Research points to a unique phenomenon: while in northern Tunisia profound transformations were evident and wide circles tended toward enlightenment and secularization, the patterns of life in Djerba remained conservative in an unprecedented manner. Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen led the effort to preserve the spiritual resilience of the community, and under his patronage local Torah creativity even developed with greater vigor during his period.[4]

1.2 Moharmakh's Central Role in Preserving the Community Character

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen not only led his community but was also the architect of its Torah defense. He was among the vigorous opponents of introducing secular and vocational studies and worked to prevent the establishment of a "Kol Israel Haverim" (Alliance Israélite Universelle) network school in Djerba.[8]

His leadership was based on a principled conception: preserving local Torah purity and educational separation (in Djerba) constituted an essential foundation for training the generation that would bear the religious-national vision. The conclusion that emerges from his work is that cultural-educational isolation, when accompanied by enormous internal Torah productivity, does not lead to decline but can cultivate a strong intellectual legacy that is not merely local.

Indeed, the power of Moharmakh's creativity extended beyond Djerba's borders. Despite living and working in an isolated community, his works became a solid foundation for halakhic decision-making for rabbis who emigrated from Djerba and its surroundings [9], and he himself gained widespread recognition among sages from various communities in Israel and the diaspora. This phenomenon demonstrates that systematic and authentic Torah creativity, such as that which Rabbi Kalfon Moshe promoted, can overcome geographical and cultural barriers and establish a broad national legacy, which serves as a focal point for scholarly convergence even many years after his death.[4, 5]

Chapter 2: His Life Story and the Transition from Study to Halakhic Decision-Making (1874–1950)

2.1 Roots, Early Education and Training

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen was born into a distinguished rabbinic family, belonging to the "Avrish" priestly families, whose family tradition traces their origin to Ezra the Scribe.[2, 3] His father was the Gaon Rabbi Shalom HaKohen of blessed memory, who was head of the rabbinical court of the town of Zarzis and composed the books Nehar Shalom (River of Peace), Hefetz Yakar (Precious Treasure), and Haim ve-Shalom (Life and Peace). His paternal grandfather was Rabbi Moshe HaKohen, author of the book Penei Moshe (Face of Moses), after whom he was named.[2]

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe's initial studies were with his father, and afterward he studied with the Gaon Rabbi Yosef BarRabi of blessed memory, who later became the rabbi of Djerba.[2, 3] Already in his youth it was evident that he was destined for greatness, and he devoted himself to his studies with great diligence.[3] At the age of twelve he moved with his father to Zarzis, where he learned the craft of ritual slaughter and examination and was appointed as a ritual slaughterer and examiner.[3] Upon reaching the age of twenty-one he married his cousin.[3]

During his lifetime, Moharmakh and his wife had seven children, among them two sons who were geniuses and authors: Rabbi Avraham Magoutz HaKohen (who died young at age 33, author of Birkat Avraham [Blessing of Abraham]) and Rabbi Shoshan HaKohen (who inherited his father's position as chief rabbi of Djerba, and later served as rabbi of Moshav Eitan in Israel).[2, 3]

2.2 The Judgeship Under Public Compulsion

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen was characterized by great humility and an aspiration to earn his living through the work of his hands. Already at age twenty-five he was offered the position of member of the rabbinical court in Djerba, but he refused, and due to his humility and willingness to work for his livelihood, he even jumped up and took an oath that he would not serve as a judge in any capacity.[3]

The story of his appointment symbolizes his profound conception of the rabbinate as a heavy yoke demanding personal sacrifice. His determined refusal and the oath testify to his understanding that this role is not intended for personal honor or comfortable livelihood, but requires total devotion.

Only after the death of the head of the Djerba rabbinical court, the Gaon Rabbi Moshe Zaken Mazouz of blessed memory, did the rabbis of Djerba and the great rabbis of Tunis return and press Rabbi Kalfon Moshe. After two years of stubborn refusal, he yielded to the public's request in the year 5677 (1917), and released himself from his oath (the details of the responsum on this matter were printed in the responsa Sho'el ve-Nish'al volume 2).[3] After accepting the position, he was appointed head of the rabbinical court of Djerba and his entire life was dedicated to dealing with "public troubles."[3]

2.3 Leadership in the Shadow of Crisis and Late Immigration

During his years of service, Rabbi Kalfon Moshe led his community in difficult times. During the period of Nazi occupation, he demonstrated courage and leadership strength that involved mortal danger, and succeeded in leading his community during that dark period.[8]

Despite public troubles, an eye disease that prevented him from writing at night, and all obstacles, Rabbi Kalfon Moshe managed to compose approximately one hundred books and pamphlets in all fields of Torah.[3]

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen died in Djerba on the eighteenth of Tevet 5710 (January 7, 1950), at age 75, on the eve of his planned immigration to the Land of Israel.[2, 10] His national vision was completed fifty-five years later, when his coffin was brought up to Israel. On the seventh of Heshvan 5766 (2005) his bones were buried on Har HaMenuhot in Jerusalem, together with Torah scrolls that had been interred with him.[3, 10]

Chapter 3: The Literary Enterprise – Analysis of the Enormous Creativity

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen left behind a comprehensive literary enterprise that included approximately one hundred diverse compositions and pamphlets in the fields of halakha, grammar, calendar calculation, ethics and ideology.[3] This extraordinary writing volume...
This dimension, formed during intensive public tenure, attests not only to genius but also to exemplary systematicity. Rabbi Kalfon Moshe emphasized in many places the importance of writing and publishing Torah novellae [3], and his literary output was an integral part of his educational and leadership system, which championed order and clarity.

3.1 The Halakhic Encyclopedia: Responsa "Sho'el ve-Nish'al"

Maharamakh's central and most comprehensive halakhic work is the series of responsa (she'elot u-teshuvot) Sho'el ve-Nish'al, comprising nine volumes.[3, 11] This series reflects the revolution the Rabbi wrought in Torah study in Djerba. Responsa literature, in which sages are asked halakhic questions by the public and provide reasoned and detailed answers [12], became in his hands a tool for changing the local study methodology. Instead of exclusive focus on "Tunisian iyyun" (intensive study of the Talmud without application to legal ruling), Rabbi Kalfon Moshe promoted systematic study of halakhic decision-making, and the series Sho'el ve-Nish'al is the representative platform of this approach.

3.2 The Foundational Pillar of Custom: "Berit Kehunah"

Another central work in his activity is Berit Kehunah, a book spanning two volumes.[3, 9] This book was dedicated entirely to one purpose: clarification, establishment, and justification of the customs of Djerba and its environs.[3]

The purpose of creating Berit Kehunah was twofold: on one hand, to serve as a binding source for legal ruling within the community, and on the other hand, to serve as a buffer against trends of halakhic standardization and foreign influences that began to penetrate Tunisia.[3] Through precise and documented codification of ancient customs, Rabbi Kalfon Moshe strengthened communal identity and gave each and every custom a well-founded halakhic stamp of approval. The book served and continues to serve to this day as a solid basis for halakhic ruling for Djerban descendants.[9]

The promotion of systematic legal ruling and the writing of Berit Kehunah can be seen not only as a technical Torah contribution but as a strategic tool for preserving communal resilience. Rabbi Kalfon Moshe fought against the Haskalah and the Alliance Israélite Universelle from a recognition that modernity brings confusion and breaching of boundaries. His practical response to these challenges was providing an internal answer of order, halakhic clarity, and absolute establishment of local tradition.

3.3 Works of Ethics and Worldview

In addition to his halakhic work, Rabbi Kalfon Moshe ha-Kohen composed many books in the areas of ethics and worldview, in which his great esteem for the teachings of Maimonides is evident.[3] Among his works is also the book Ḥuqot Moshe, intended to serve as statute and law for a scattered flock, while addressing public and communal problems.[9]

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe's ethical conception focused inter alia on the formative power of speech. He taught that words a person says aloud not only reveal his feelings and thoughts but penetrate his heart and shape his inner self.[8] This is a conception that places supreme responsibility on every act of speech.

The scope and types of Rabbi Kalfon Moshe ha-Kohen's work are summarized in the following table:

Table 1: Scope and Types of the Torah Work of Rabbi Kalfon Moshe ha-Kohen (Maharamakh)

Chapter 4: His Halakhic Teaching – Ruling Between Maran and Djerban Custom

4.1 The Pedagogical Revolution and Training of Legal Decisors

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe ha-Kohen effected a fundamental revolution in the methods of Torah study in Djerba. While his predecessors engaged primarily in "Tunisian iyyun" – intensive Talmud study – he promoted extensive and systematic study of halakhic ruling.[8]

His study method on Sabbaths was a striking example of his educational approach. He presented a halakhic problem on which his students labored during the week and formulated an answer. On the Sabbath they discussed the matter while he examined their answers. This method, which was systematic and thorough, produced a cadre of decisors skilled in halakhah.[8] His distinguished student, the Gaon Rabbi Raḥamim Ḥai Ḥavita ha-Kohen, inherited his position as Av Beit Din of Djerba.[3]

4.2 The Balance Between the Shulḥan Arukh and Djerban Tradition

In his halakhic rulings, and especially in his responsa books, Rabbi Kalfon Moshe adopted a method combining absolute fidelity to two foundations that were sometimes contradictory:

Acceptance of Maran's rulings: On one hand, Rabbi Kalfon Moshe accepted the rulings of Maran of the Shulḥan Arukh, and argued that they "cannot be nullified even by one thousand".[3]

Preservation of ancient customs: On the other hand, he refused to relinquish the ancient and established customs of the Jewish community of the island of Djerba.[3]

The central tool that served this balance was the book Berit Kehunah. Through this book, he was careful to establish each and every custom to ensure its precise preservation, and thereby made custom an integral and reasoned part of legal ruling. This approach, which united central authority (Maran) with local legitimacy (custom), ensured continuation of Djerba's traditional path.

4.3 Priority of Redemption of the Land Over Custom

Another fascinating topic in his halakhic worldview concerns the commandment of settling the Land of Israel. Rabbi Kalfon Moshe was willing to use the power of legal ruling to be lenient in halakhah and in the community's ancient customs for the sake of a supreme national-religious goal: facilitating immigration to the Land of Israel.[8]

The fact that a figure who supported so absolutely and uncompromisingly the preservation of ancestral customs, to the point of writing two foundational volumes on them [3, 9], was willing to relinquish them for the sake of redemption of the Land, indicates that the position of the commandment of return to Zion in his halakhic worldview was higher than any stringency or custom. This position proves that Zionism was not for him an external political stance but an integral and constitutive part of his halakhic teaching, which dictated new orders of priority in light of the sparks of redemption.

Chapter 5: His Ideological Teaching – Zionism, Ethics, and Universalism

5.1 Rooted Zionism and Torah Nationalism

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe ha-Kohen was known as an ardent Zionist. He saw the Balfour Declaration, ratified at the San Remo Conference, as "sparks of redemption".[8] His intense love for the Land of Israel found frequent expression in his writings, in which he expressed intense longing for Zion and the inheritance of his fathers.[3, 10] In his book Zekhut Moshe, he wrote: "Through the oath we swore to always remember our land and the inheritance of our fathers, Jerusalem... therefore it always seems to us as if it has just now been destroyed, and as if we have just now departed from it".[10]

Nevertheless, it is important to emphasize the unique character of this Zionism. As Rabbi Meir Mazuz clarified, the Zionism of Maharamakh was not "secular Zionism," but rather nationalism entirely anchored in Torah, like the teaching of Rabbi Yehudah Halevi, intended to join religion and nationalism together in the pure sense of the word.[13] His death on the eve of his immigration [2], and the bringing of his bones to Jerusalem, symbolize the completion of his national vision after his death.

5.2 Humility, Social Justice, and the Ethics of Leadership

Although Rabbi Kalfon Moshe was known as one who stood firmly against breakers of boundaries, he was also known for his great humility.[3] A central example demonstrating his ethical conception and his humanitarian considerations is his relinquishment of the stringency of eating shemura matzah, a stringency he practiced for years, after he discovered that this stringency would not be accessible to the general public desiring it.[8] This deed expresses the principle of social justice and leadership that places the good of the collective and accessibility of the commandment before personal stringencies.

His teaching concerning the power of speech, according to which the words a person says aloud not only reveal his thoughts but also penetrate his heart and shape his personality [8], presents the emphasis he placed on child education and speech ethics.

5.3 Universal Vision – World Law from Zion

Alongside his engagement with halakhah and guarding communal boundaries, Rabbi Kalfon Moshe ha-Kohen developed a broad-scope ideological vision concerning world peace. In his works, he expressed support for establishing the League of Nations (an organization that preceded the UN) and proposed establishing an international court whose center would be in Jerusalem.[8]

This conception, voiced by the leader of an isolated and conservative community, is not a contradiction to his character but part of a visionary hierarchy. Rabbi Kalfon Moshe saw in preserving local Torah purity (in Djerba) the foundation for training the generation that would bear the banner of religious nationalism (Zionism), which w
and worked in his generation for the repair of the world. The establishment of a universal rabbinical court in Jerusalem was perceived as the realization of the prophetic vision ("For out of Zion shall go forth the Torah, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem"), and expresses the belief that the Torah of Israel is the key to universal justice and law.

Chapter 6: Summary and Conclusions – His Eternal Legacy and His Evaluation in Subsequent Generations

6.1 Summary of His Historical and Torah Activity

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen fulfilled a decisive role in preserving the identity of Djerban Jewry in the face of the challenges of modernity and French influence.[4] His principal Torah activity included two central pillars:

The methodological transformation: Leading the transition from "iyyun" alone to systematic study of halakhic decisors, thereby establishing a cadre of new poskim.[8]

The codification: The creation of massive literary projects (approximately one hundred books), foremost among them the responsa She'elot Sho'el ve-Nish'al (Questions Asked and Answered) and the monumental customs compendium Berit Kehunah (Covenant of the Priesthood).[3, 9] This oeuvre provided a stable halakhic framework for the community and transformed custom into a reasoned component of halakhic decision-making.[3]

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen served as Av Bet Din of Djerba between the years 1917 and 1950.[3] His position in the rabbinic dynasty of Djerba is presented in the following table:

Table 2: The Position of Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen on the Timeline of the Rabbis of Djerba

6.2 The Esteem from the Luminaries of Subsequent Generations and His Legacy in the Diaspora

Recognition of the greatness of Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen transcends the boundaries of the Djerban community. His works entered the general Torah canon and he received enthusiastic appreciation from the luminaries of subsequent generations, from across the entire Torah spectrum. Maran Rabbi Ovadiah Yosef zt"l praised his work.[3] Particularly notable is the esteem of Maran the Rosh Yeshiva, the Gaon Rabbi Meir Mazuz shlita, who called Moharamakh "the genius of the generation, the giant of the generation in wisdom, understanding, ethics, fear of Heaven, uprightness, righteousness, truth and humility—none like him has arisen!".[3, 14] Rabbi Mazuz added and determined that although he lived all his days in a small community in Djerba, "there is almost none like him in the world".[3]

The esteem which Rabbi Kalfon Moshe received, both from the great rabbis of our generation and from academic research institutions that hold conferences and publish volumes on his work [4, 5], attests to acceptance and recognition that transcends sectors and disciplines. He left behind a dual legacy: halakhic leadership that became the foundation of the halakhic rulings of entire communities, and a model for traditional rabbinate that knew how to contend in a sophisticated manner with modernity. He not only stemmed external influences but created a profound internal response that transformed him into a key figure in modern Jewish history.

Rabbi Kalfon Moshe HaKohen offers a unique model: a leader who was a penetrating halakhist and adherent of ancestral custom, yet at the same time possessed a national and even universal vision, combining personal humility with public assertiveness, and who provided preemptive remedy by constructing an internal Torah system that would sustain the community for generations.
